The authors conclude, while rating the evidence low quality, that olanzapine or quetiapine may be a preferred antipsychotic (abstract and last discussion paragraph). Editors' arithmetic from Table 2A and Fig. 3A: the direct comparisons form a chain without a closed loop, so indirect estimates are sums of single-trial estimates (olanzapine vs risperidone −1.09 = olanzapine vs haloperidol −0.49 plus haloperidol vs risperidone −0.60; quetiapine vs risperidone −0.86 = −0.26 plus −0.60), and both advantages over risperidone rest on the one open-label haloperidol–risperidone trial (Samiei 2016, 22 and 22 participants).

Use and symptoms were self-reported at the same interviews, over different windows at the first three: use of methamphetamine or other amphetamine-type stimulants (the question named speed, P and ice) since the previous interview at every wave; psychotic symptom items from the SCL-90 for the past month at ages 18, 21 and 25, and from the Diagnostic Interview Schedule for the period since the previous assessment at 30 and 35 (the authors say the difference in time frames was corrected in the analyses, without saying how); 35.2%, 41.8% and 36.4% reported at least one symptom in the periods to age 25; the authors note that some SCL-90 items arguably do not capture genuine psychotic experiences.

E-value 1.571 (confidence limit 1.11) for unmeasured confounding; population attributable fraction 8.0% (2.2%–14.7%), which the methods define as assuming causality. The authors conclude that methamphetamine use is an independent risk factor for psychosis in the general population, on self-reported symptom items reported at the same interviews as use.

Groups depart from the stated criteria: the primary psychotic disorder group in Hides 2015 (20 people) was drawn from 198 people who had used methamphetamine in the previous month; Hajebi 2018 compared first-episode primary psychosis (reference title) although first-episode psychosis was an exclusion criterion. The criteria themselves admit both persistent psychosis after recent cessation and psychosis with current use, so the methamphetamine-psychosis groups mix the two; six studies reported other substance use; the authors state that the cross-sectional designs allow no causal interpretation.
